---
title: "A straight-line mean"
---

The [preceding page](regression-models.qmd) represented a regression through its conditional mean function $m(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$. We now impose one restriction on that function.

Suppose we represent the conditional mean of log reading time as

$$
m(x)=\beta_0+\beta_1x.
$$

This is the mean function for [**simple linear regression**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=85). It contains one predictor and two coefficients.

The word *simple* refers to the number of predictors, not to the linguistic
question or the difficulty of fitting the model. The word *linear* refers to the
way the coefficients enter the mean function. With one predictor, that function
is a straight line.

## Read the intercept

Set $x=0$:

$$
m(0)=\beta_0+\beta_1(0)=\beta_0.
$$

The intercept $\beta_0$ is the expected response when the predictor equals zero.

If $\beta_0=5.70$, the model assigns expected log reading time 5.70 to a word with surprisal 0 bits. Whether that reference point is linguistically informative depends on the observed predictor range.

An intercept remains part of the equation even when zero lies outside the
observed range. It locates the line. But its linguistic interpretation may then
depend on extrapolation. If the study contains words between 2 and 9 bits, the
data do not directly show the response distribution at 0 bits.

## Read the slope

Compare the mean at $x$ with the mean one unit higher:

$$
\begin{aligned}
m(x+1)-m(x)
&=[\beta_0+\beta_1(x+1)]-[\beta_0+\beta_1x]\\
&=\beta_1.
\end{aligned}
$$

The slope $\beta_1$ is the change in expected response for a one-unit increase in the predictor.

If $\beta_1=.06$, one additional bit of surprisal is associated with a $.06$ increase in expected log reading time.

The coefficient has units. Here it is measured in log milliseconds per bit. If
surprisal were measured in nats instead of bits, the numerical coefficient would
change because one unit on the predictor scale would represent a different
amount of information.

The sign determines the direction:

| slope | mean pattern |
|---:|---|
| $\beta_1>0$ | expected response increases with $x$ |
| $\beta_1=0$ | expected response does not change with $x$ |
| $\beta_1<0$ | expected response decreases with $x$ |

The slope also determines differences across larger predictor changes. For two
values $x_a$ and $x_b$,

$$
m(x_b)-m(x_a)=\beta_1(x_b-x_a).
$$

With $\beta_1=.06$, a four-bit contrast corresponds to an expected log-time
difference of $.24$. This is the same result whether the comparison is from 3 to
7 bits or from 4 to 8 bits. The constant slope is the principal constraint of
the straight-line mean.

## Calculate a small prediction table

Take $\beta_0=5.70$ and $\beta_1=.06$. Then

| surprisal $x$ | calculation | conditional mean $m(x)$ |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | $5.70+.06(2)$ | $5.82$ |
| 5 | $5.70+.06(5)$ | $6.00$ |
| 8 | $5.70+.06(8)$ | $6.18$ |

The three points lie on one line. The increase from 2 to 5 bits is $.18$, and
the increase from 5 to 8 bits is also $.18$. A different pattern, such as a
sharp increase only above 7 bits, cannot be represented by this mean function.

## Add observation-level variation

The line specifies only a conditional mean. Individual reading times still vary around it.

Ordinary linear regression adds a normally distributed error term:

$$
Y_i\mid X_i=x_i
\sim
\mathcal{N}(\beta_0+\beta_1x_i,\sigma^2).
$$

Equivalently,

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\varepsilon_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2).
$$

The coefficients describe systematic change in the conditional mean. The parameter $\sigma$ describes response variation around that mean, assumed constant across predictor values.

For a word with 5 bits of surprisal, the expected response is 6.00 under the
worked model. The normal distribution says that an individual log reading time
may fall above or below 6.00. If $\sigma=.20$, an observed value of 6.14 is not a
contradiction. It is one possible realization from a distribution centered at
6.00.

We can simulate six responses at declared predictor values:

```{r}
#| label: simulate-simple-linear-responses
#| echo: true
set.seed(214)

x <- c(2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8)
conditional_mean <- 5.70 + .06 * x
y <- rnorm(length(x), mean = conditional_mean, sd = .20)

data.frame(
  surprisal = x,
  conditional_mean = conditional_mean,
  simulated_response = y
)
```

The conditional means lie exactly on the declared line. The simulated responses
do not. Regression represents both facts: systematic change in the center and
unexplained variation around that center.

Thus the complete model makes three commitments:

1. the conditional mean is linear;
2. responses around that mean are normally distributed; and
3. the conditional response variance is the same at every $x$.

It also inherits a sampling commitment from the earlier inference pages. The
observations are treated as conditionally independent under this simple model.
Repeated words from the same participant or repeated observations of the same
item may violate that claim. The equation does not stop being linear, but the
complete probability model is then missing the repeated structure.

## Separate a line from a causal claim

A positive $\beta_1$ describes a conditional association under the model. It
does not by itself show that surprisal causes longer reading times. Word length,
frequency, position, and other lexical or contextual properties may vary with
surprisal.

Moving from a fitted association to a causal statement requires a design-based identification argument. Adding a normal response
distribution or estimating the slope precisely does not supply that argument. A
causal claim needs a design or identification argument that distinguishes the
proposed cause from alternative sources of the association.

::: {.callout-note title="Calculate two means"}
1. If $\beta_0=5.70$ and $\beta_1=.06$, calculate $m(3)$ and $m(7)$. How much
   does the expected response change across that four-bit difference?
2. Why does a conditional mean of 6.00 not require every observed response at
   that predictor value to equal 6.00?
3. Give one response pattern that a straight-line mean cannot represent.
4. Explain why the fitted surprisal association does not by itself license a causal interpretation.
:::

The [centering page](centering-predictors.qmd) changes the reference value for the intercept without changing this fitted line.
